claim_verdicts.evidence: Round 2: wording now 'one method', steps 'typically', 'a script may skip a step' — resolves round-1 minor (fixed order). Still no allowed source defines Transaction Script; refs/dotnet-docs microservice-domain-model.md:42 supports only the 'data holds no rules' half: 'service objects ... capture all the domain or business logic ... uses the data model just as data.' Kind fact, non-blocking.

Origin is indirectly supported: dotnet docs link 'transaction scripts' to martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/transactionScript.html, and EF6 testability article cites 'Catalog of Patterns from Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture'. The book itself is not an allowed source; nothing under refs/ states that 'transaction' in the name means a business operation. Kind history, non-blocking.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs lines 29-38: FindAsync(orderId) ?? throw new KeyNotFoundException; order.Status = "cancelled"; await repository.SaveChangesAsync(); notifier.Send(order.Id, "order cancelled"). No read of order.Status before the assignment.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs lines 8-23: if (items.Count == 0) throw new ArgumentException(...); new Order { CustomerId, PlacedAt, Status = "new", Items }; AddAsync; SaveChangesAsync; notifier.Send(order.Id, "order placed").

Entities.cs@stage-1 25-35: Order has Id, CustomerId, PlacedAt, Status, Items, Customer, each { get; set; }, no method. git grep -i 'shipped|.Status' stage-1 -- '*.cs' (excl. tests): the only status write outside the entity is OrderService.cs:34; OrdersController.cs:55,61 only read Status into DTOs. So 'has no place in Order, so in this design it is written in the script' holds; the round-1 overstatement 'can only live in the script' is gone.

git grep -i transaction stage-1 -- '*.cs' → no match (no BeginTransaction/TransactionScope). EfOrderRepository.FindAsync = FirstOrDefaultAsync (own query); SaveChangesAsync = db.SaveChangesAsync. EF Core: 'all changes in a single call to SaveChanges are applied in a transaction'; 'You can use the DbContext.Database API to begin, commit, and rollback transactions'; example uses context.Database.BeginTransaction(). No explicit transaction → none spans query + save.
OrderService.cs@stage-1 lines 25-28: '// Deliberately missing a check: an order already `shipped` still gets // cancelled here. `DonHang.Tests` covers `new` but not `shipped` —'.

dotnet docs: 'if you need to tackle the complexity of a microservice's domain that has a lot of ever-changing business rules, the anemic domain model might be an anti-pattern'. The 'own copy of the check' part follows from the code: Order (Entities.cs:25-35) has no method, so a status check can only be written per caller; CancelOrderAsync has none.

Round 2: 'the simplest design' → 'a simple design that works well while operations share few rules' — superlative removed, condition kept. dotnet docs support the condition only: 'if your microservice or Bounded Context is very simple (a CRUD service), the anemic domain model ... might be good enough'. 'often clearer' remains hedged opinion with a condition; non-blocking.

Ran: git grep -n "Status" stage-1 -- "DonHang.Domain/*.cs" → 'DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs:30:    public required string Status { get; set; }', 'DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs:16:            Status = "new",', 'DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs:34:        order.Status = "cancelled";'. Exactly three lines.

db/schema.sql@stage-1: status CHECK (status IN ('new','paid','shipped','cancelled')). git grep ShipOrder stage-1 → no match. Section 2 no longer names 'paid'; the ledger's value list is wider than the text but still true.
